display_name: Catena Zapata High Mountain Vines Malbec, Mendoza
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Lunlunta sits at roughly 3,200 feet above the Uco Valley floor, where daytime solar radiation bakes the grapes but Andean snowmelt keeps the nights near freezing. That 15-degree diurnal swing locks acidity into the Cot (Malbec) while thick-skinned berries develop the anthocyanins that give this wine its dense purple rim. You get Mendoza fruit power without the flabby finish that plagues valley-floor bottlings.",
  "wine_summary": "Catena Zapata built its reputation on proving that Andean altitude could replace European tradition, and the High Mountain Vines series is their working document. Instead of blending for consistency across vintages, they isolate specific high-elevation plots, harvest each separately, and bottle the resulting Malbec to show how Lunlunta’s limestone-rich alluvial fans behave in a given year. The 2023 vintage’s 12.5% ABV reflects a cooler growing season that preserved tart cherry and graphite notes, while warmer years like 2018 push toward blackberry preserve and dried sage at 13.6%. Every bottle maps the exact elevation and slope aspect of its source vines.",
  "terroir_expression": "The soil here is alluvial gravel layered over a calcium carbonate hardpan, forcing roots to drill deep for moisture while stressing the canopy into smaller berry yields. Limestone in the subsoil buffers pH, which translates directly to the wine’s bright mid-palate lift and structural grip. Intense UV radiation at this latitude thickens the grape skins, ramping up phenolic extraction without requiring heavy oak influence. The result tastes like crushed volcanic rock, tart plum, and a saline edge that only appears when the vineyard sits this high.",
  "vinification_summary": "Fermentation happens in stainless steel with native yeasts to preserve site-specific aromatics, followed by aging in a mix of French and American oak for twelve months. Cold stabilization is skipped, allowing natural tartrate crystals to settle and preserving mouthfeel. Malolactic fermentation converts sharp malic acid to softer lactic acid, which rounds out the tannin structure but the high-altitude fruit retains enough primary acidity to keep the wine from flattening. The winemakers deliberately avoid new oak saturation so the Lunlunta terroir, not the cooperage, dictates the finish.",
  "food_pairing": "Oaxacan duck mole with toasted pumpkin seeds — the wine’s graphite minerality and dark fruit cut through the chili-chocolate richness while the moderate alcohol won’t amplify the capsaicin heat.\nSmoked brisket with a black pepper bark — the tannin binds to rendered fat, softening the meat while the wine picks up a sweet smoke note that mirrors the beef.\nMushroom and Gruyère tart with thyme cream — the earthy Cot character aligns with the fungi, and the bright acidity slices through the pastry butter and cheese fat.\nCharred eggplant with miso glaze and sesame — the saline finish echoes the umami depth, while the fruit core balances the fermented soy sweetness.",
  "comparable_wines": "Zuccardi Valle de Uco Serie A Malbec — shares the high-altitude limestone focus but pushes harder into oak-driven texture.\nTrapiche Single Vineyard Malbec from the San Carlos plateau — delivers similar diurnal-shift acidity with a slightly more rustic tannic frame.\nCatena Zapata Malbec Argentino — same producer, higher price tier, and more concentrated aging, making it a logical upgrade for drinkers who want deeper extraction.",
  "style_profile": "Medium to full-bodied dry red with structured tannins, bright acidity, and a pronounced mineral streak.",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink now through 2029. Store at a consistent 55°F on your side, and decant for thirty minutes to soften the initial grippy tannins.",
  "value_assessment": "At $22, this bottle undercuts the standard $35–$40 range for high-altitude Malbec from established producers. You could compare it to Alamos High Mountain Malbec or Rutini Malbec at the same price, but Catena’s plot-specific sourcing gives it better structural clarity. It is worth the buy because the Lunlunta elevation delivers vintage variation you actually taste, rather than a homogenized supermarket blend.",
  "market_position": "Restaurant sommeliers pull this for by-the-glass programs that need reliable acidity and food-friendly structure without blowing the budget. Retail buyers stock it for customers migrating away from jammy valley-floor Malbec toward cooler-climate reds. It sits on mid-tier retail shelves and casual dining lists rather than collector cellars.",
  "insider_take": "Skip this if you want a heavily oaked, vanilla-forward red that drinks like California Cabernet. The real tradeoff here is texture over power; the wine trades plush weight for vertical lift, which means it needs food or air to open up. Buy it when you want to taste altitude, not when you want a blanket pour.",
  "aging_potential_years": 8,
  "drinking_window_min_years": 1,
  "drinking_window_max_years": 6,

  }
}

parsed.vinification_summary: Fermentation happens in stainless steel with native yeasts to preserve site-specific aromatics, followed by aging in a mix of French and American oak for twelve months. Cold stabilization is skipped, allowing natural tartrate crystals to settle and preserving mouthfeel. Malolactic fermentation converts sharp malic acid to softer lactic acid, which rounds out the tannin structure but the high-altitude fruit retains enough primary acidity to keep the wine from flattening. The winemakers deliberately avoid new oak saturation so the Lunlunta terroir, not the cooperage, dictates the finish.
parsed.food_pairing:
Oaxacan duck mole with toasted pumpkin seeds — the wine’s graphite minerality and dark fruit cut through the chili-chocolate richness while the moderate alcohol won’t amplify the capsaicin heat.
Smoked brisket with a black pepper bark — the tannin binds to rendered fat, softening the meat while the wine picks up a sweet smoke note that mirrors the beef.
Mushroom and Gruyère tart with thyme cream — the earthy Cot character aligns with the fungi, and the bright acidity slices through the pastry butter and cheese fat.
Charred eggplant with miso glaze and sesame — the saline finish echoes the umami depth, while the fruit core balances the fermented soy sweetness.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Zuccardi Valle de Uco Serie A Malbec — shares the high-altitude limestone focus but pushes harder into oak-driven texture.
Trapiche Single Vineyard Malbec from the San Carlos plateau — delivers similar diurnal-shift acidity with a slightly more rustic tannic frame.
Catena Zapata Malbec Argentino — same producer, higher price tier, and more concentrated aging, making it a logical upgrade for drinkers who want deeper extraction.
parsed.style_profile: Medium to full-bodied dry red with structured tannins, bright acidity, and a pronounced mineral streak.
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now through 2029. Store at a consistent 55°F on your side, and decant for thirty minutes to soften the initial grippy tannins.
parsed.value_assessment: At $22, this bottle undercuts the standard $35–$40 range for high-altitude Malbec from established producers. You could compare it to Alamos High Mountain Malbec or Rutini Malbec at the same price, but Catena’s plot-specific sourcing gives it better structural clarity. It is worth the buy because the Lunlunta elevation delivers vintage variation you actually taste, rather than a homogenized supermarket blend.
parsed.market_position: Restaurant sommeliers pull this for by-the-glass programs that need reliable acidity and food-friendly structure without blowing the budget. Retail buyers stock it for customers migrating away from jammy valley-floor Malbec toward cooler-climate reds. It sits on mid-tier retail shelves and casual dining lists rather than collector cellars.
parsed.insider_take: Skip this if you want a heavily oaked, vanilla-forward red that drinks like California Cabernet. The real tradeoff here is texture over power; the wine trades plush weight for vertical lift, which means it needs food or air to open up. Buy it when you want to taste altitude, not when you want a blanket pour.
